DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilg.gov.ph DILG OPINION No. 120 s. 2021 OCT ZI 2021 ATTY. ANTHONY C. NUYDA Regional Director, DILG- Region V Rizal St., Legazpi City Dear Regional Director Nuyda: This refers to your letter requesting the Central Office to confirm the legality of the tax imposed by the Province of Camarines Note under Section 25, in relation to Section 28, of its Provincial Ordinance No. 31-2015 (PO 31-2015), otherwise known as the Revenue Code of Camarines Norte. As guidance, Section 25 and 28 of PO 31-2015 states as follows: "ARTICLE D TAX ON SAND, GRAVEL AND OTHER QUARRY RESOURCES Section 25. Imposition of Tax. There is levied, as fixed provincial tax, ten percent (10%) of the fair market value in the locality of each cubic meter of ordinary stones, sand, gravel, earth and other quarry resources, as defined under the National Internal Revenue Code, as amended which are extracted from public and private lands or from beds of seas, lakes, rivers, streams, creeks and other public waters within the territorial jurisdiction of the province. Section 28. Time and Place of Payment. The tax shall be due and payable to the Provincial Treasurer or his authorized representatives upon approval of the Provincial Governor of the permit to extract the above-mentioned materials and the issuance of the Governor's Permit and before materials are taken or removed." Your office claims that the tax imposed by Camarines Norte under Section 25, in relation to Section 28, imposes tax on: (a) the person or entity extracting the materials (i.e. quarry operators); and (b) the materials extracted themselves; thereby constituting double taxation. "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

The Central Office is of the view that the tax imposed under Section 25, in relation to Section 28, of PO 31-2015 does not constitute double taxation on the quarry operators and the materials extracted. It is simply a tax imposed on the materials themselves authorized by the Local Government Code of 1991 (LGC). Section 25 of PO 31-2015 finds its foundation on Section 138 of the LGC, which states: "Section 138. Tax on Sand, Gravel and Other Quarry Resources. - The province may levy and collect not more than ten percent (10%) of fair market value in the locality per cubic meter of ordinary stones, sand, gravel, earth, and other quarry resources, as defined under the National Internal Revenue Code, as amended, extracted from public lands or from the beds of seas, lakes, rivers, streams, creeks, and other public waters within its territorial jurisdiction. The permit to extract sand, gravel and other quarry resources shall be issued exclusively by the provincial governor, pursuant to the ordinance of the sangguniang panlalawigan. The proceeds of the tax on sand, gravel and other quarry resources shall be distributed as follows: (I)Province - Thirty percent (30%); (2)Component City or Municipality where the sand, gravel, and other quarry resources are extracted - Thirty percent (30%); and (3) Barangay where the sand, gravel, and other quarry resources are extracted - Forty percent (40%)." A province may therefore levy taxes on stones, sand, gravel, earth and other quarry resources extracted from public land because it is expressly empowered to do so under the LGC. It is further authorized to issue permits for the said extraction. Such authority was duly clarified and confirmed by the Supreme Court in Lepanto Consolidated Mining Company vs. Hon. Mauricio B. Ambanlocl, to wit: Lepanto relies on the principle that when a company is taxed on its main business, it is no longer taxable for engaging in an activity that is but a part of, incidental to, and necessary to such main business. Lepanto points out that, since it did not extract and use sand and gravel as independent activities but as integral parts of its mining operations, it should not be subjected to a separate tax on the same. But in the cases where this principle has been applied, the taxes which were stricken down were in the nature of business taxes. The reasoning behind those cases was that the incidental activity could not be treated as a business separate and distinct from the main business of the taxpayer. Here the tax is an excise tax imposed on the privilege of extracting sand and gravel. And it is settled that provincial governments can levy excise taxes on quarry IG.R. No. 180639, 29 June 2010 page 2 of 3

resources independently from the national government." (Emphasis supplied) In view of the foregoing, it is the considered position of this Department that the tax imposed by the Province of Camarines Norte under Section 25 and 28 of its PO 31- 2015 does not constitute double taxation. However, Section 138 of the LGC, authorizes provinces to impose taxes on quarry resources obtained from public lands and public waters only. Section 25 of PO 31- 2015, on the other hand, levies the said tax on quarry resources which are derived from both private and public land. We respectfully submit that while Section 25 of PO 31-2015 does not constitute double taxation on the quarry operators and the materials extracted as earlier mentioned, it was nonetheless issued in excess of the province's authority under the LGC insofar as quarry resources from private lands are taxed. It may thus be annulled through the institution of an appropriate action before the proper courts of Camarines Norte. As held by the Supreme Coutt in The Province of Bulacan, et. al. vs. Court of Appeals and Republic Cement (G.R. No. 126232, 27 November 1998): "Furthermore, Section 21 of Provincial Ordinance No. 3 is practically only a reproduction of Section 138 of the Local Government Code. A cursory reading of both would show that both refer to ordinary sand, stone, gravel, earth and other quarry resources extracted from public lands. Even if we disregard the limitation set by Section 133 of the Local Government Code, petitioners may not, impose taxes on stones, sand, gravel, earth and other quarry resources extracted from private lands on the basis of Section 21 of Provincial Ordinance No. 3 as the latter clearly applies only to quarry resources extracted from public lands. Petitioners may not invoke the Regalian doctrine to extend the coverage of their ordinance to quarry resources extracted from private lands, for taxes, being burdens, are not to be presumed beyond what the applicable statute expressly and clearly declares, tax statutes being construed strictissimi juris against the government." This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have sufficiently addressed your concerns. Thank you. Very truly yours, By Authority of the Secretary: RLO I I GAN Underse tary for Local Government OUSLG/MLl/LLLS-LRALLD/kuq/c1p Page 3 of 3
